paragraphs: So he spoke, and Agamemnon listened to his words. At once he sent the criers around to summon the people to assembly. They called, and the people gathered. The chiefs around the son of Atreus picked out their men and set them in order, while Athena moved among them holding her priceless aegis, which never ages and never dies. A hundred tassels of pure gold hung from it, all finely woven, and each one was worth a hundred oxen. With this she darted furiously everywhere through the armies of the Achaeans, urging them on and putting courage into every man’s heart, so that he would fight and do battle without rest. War became sweeter to them than returning home in their ships. As a great forest fire rages on a mountaintop and its light is seen from far away, so the gleam of their armor, as they marched, flashed up into the sky of heaven.

They were like great flocks of geese, or cranes, or swans on the plain by the waters of Cayster. The birds fly this way and that, proud of their flight, and cry out as they settle, until the marsh is alive with their screaming. In the same way the tribes poured from the ships and tents onto the plain of the Scamander, and the ground rang like brass under the feet of men and horses. They stood on the flower-covered field as thick as the leaves that come out in summer.
As countless swarms of flies buzz around a herdsman’s farmyard in springtime, when the pails are drenched with milk, so the Achaeans swarmed onto the plain to charge the Trojans and destroy them.

The chiefs sorted their men this way and that before the fight began, as easily as goatherds sort their flocks when they have got mixed while feeding. Among them went King Agamemnon. His head and face were like Zeus the lord of thunder, his waist like Ares, and his chest like Poseidon’s. A great bull stands out above the herds on the plain and lords it over them. In the same way Zeus made the son of Atreus stand out beyond all others in the crowd of heroes.

And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell me—for you are goddesses, you are in all places and see all things, while we know nothing except by report—who were the chiefs and princes of the Danaans? As for the common soldiers, I could not name every one of them, even if I had ten tongues, a voice that never failed and a heart of bronze within me, unless you, Olympian Muses, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus, were to recount them to me. Still, I will name the captains of the ships and all the ships together.

The Boeotians had five captains: Peneleos, Leitus, Arcesilaus, Prothoenor and Clonius. Their people lived in Hyria and rocky Aulis. They held Schoenus, Scolus and the highlands of Eteonus, along with Thespeia, Graia and the fair city of Mycalessus. Harma, Eilesium and Erythrae were theirs too, as were Eleon, Hyle and Peteon; Ocalea and the strong fortress of Medeon; Copae, Eutresis and Thisbe the haunt of doves; Coronea and the pastures of Haliartus; Plataea and Glisas; the fortress of Thebes the less; holy Onchestus with its famous grove of Poseidon; Arne rich in vineyards; Midea, sacred Nisa, and Anthedon on the sea. Fifty ships sailed from these places, and each carried a hundred and twenty young Boeotian men.

Ascalaphus and Ialmenus, sons of Ares, led the people of Aspledon and Orchomenus, the realm of Minyas. A noble maiden, Astyoche, bore them in the house of Actor son of Azeus. She had gone secretly to an upper room with Ares, and he had lain with her. Thirty ships came with these men.

Schedius and Epistrophus led the Phoceans. They were sons of mighty Iphitus, the son of Naubolus. Their people held Cyparissus, rocky Pytho, holy Crisa, Daulis and Panopeus. Also with them were those who lived in Anemorea and Hyampolis, around the waters of the river Cephissus, and in Lilaea by the springs of the Cephissus. Forty ships came with their chieftains, and the chieftains drew up the forces of the Phoceans, who were stationed next to the Boeotians, on their left.

Ajax, the swift son of Oileus, commanded the Locrians. He was not so great as Ajax the son of Telamon, nor nearly so. He was a little man, and his breastplate was made of linen, but with the spear he surpassed all the Hellenes and the Achaeans. His people lived in Cynus, Opous, Calliarus, Bessa, Scarphe, fair Augeae, Tarphe and Thronium, around the river Boagrius. Forty ships of the Locrians who live beyond Euboea came with him.

The fierce Abantes held Euboea with its cities: Chalcis, Eretria, Histiaea rich in vines, Cerinthus on the sea, and the rock-perched town of Dium. With them were also the men of Carystus and Styra. Elephenor of the race of Ares commanded them. He was the son of Chalcodon and chief over all the Abantes. They followed him, swift-footed and wearing their hair long behind, brave warriors who always fought to tear open their enemies’ corslets with their long ashen spears. Fifty ships came from these.

Then there were those who held the strong city of Athens, the people of great Erechtheus. He was born of the soil itself, but Zeus’s daughter Athena fostered him and set him up at Athens, in her own rich sanctuary. There the Athenian youths worship him year by year with sacrifices of bulls and rams. Menestheus, son of Peteos, commanded them. No man alive could equal him at marshalling chariots and foot soldiers. Only Nestor could rival him, because Nestor was older. Fifty ships came with him.
Ajax brought twelve ships from Salamis and stationed them beside those of the Athenians.

Then came the men of Argos, and those who held the walls of Tiryns, with Hermione and Asine on the gulf; Troezene, Eionae and the vineyard lands of Epidaurus; and the Achaean youths who came from Aegina and Mases. Diomedes of the loud battle cry led them, with Sthenelus son of famed Capaneus. Euryalus also commanded them, son of king Mecisteus, son of Talaus; but Diomedes was chief over them all. Eighty ships came with these.

Those who held the strong city of Mycenae, rich Corinth and Cleonae; Orneae, Araethyrea and Licyon, where Adrastus reigned long ago; Hyperesia, high Gonoessa and Pellene; Aegium and all the coastland around Helice: these sent a hundred ships under King Agamemnon, son of Atreus. His force was by far the finest and the most numerous. In the midst of them was the king himself, glorious in his armor of gleaming bronze. He stood foremost among the heroes, because he was the greatest king and had the most men under him.

And those who lived in Lacedaemon, lying low among the hills: Pharis, Sparta, and Messe the haunt of doves; Bryseae, Augeae, Amyclae and Helos on the sea; also Laas and Oetylus. Menelaus of the loud battle cry, Agamemnon’s brother, led them, and they had sixty ships, drawn up apart from the others. Menelaus himself went among them, strong in zeal, urging his men to fight. He longed to avenge the toil and sorrow he had suffered for Helen’s sake.

The men of Pylos and Arene, and Thryum where the ford of the river Alpheus is; strong Aipy, Cyparisseis and Amphigenea; Pteleum, Helos and Dorium, where the Muses met Thamyris and silenced his minstrelsy forever. He was returning from Oechalia, where Eurytus lived and reigned, and he boasted that he would surpass even the Muses, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus, if they should sing against him. The Muses were angry and maimed him. They robbed him of his divine power of song, and from then on he could strike the lyre no more. Nestor, knight of Gerene, commanded these men, and ninety ships came with him.

And those who held Arcadia, under the high mountain of Cyllene, near the tomb of Aepytus, where the people fight hand to hand; the men of Pheneus also, and Orchomenus rich in flocks; of Rhipae, Stratie and bleak Enispe; of Tegea and fair Mantinea; of Stymphelus and Parrhasia. King Agapenor son of Ancaeus commanded these, and they had sixty ships. Many Arcadians, good soldiers, came in each one. But Agamemnon supplied the ships in which they would cross the sea, because they were not a people who busied themselves with the water.

The men of Buprasium and of Elis, as much of it as lies between Hyrmine, Myrsinus on the seashore, the rock Olene and Alesium. They had four leaders, each with ten ships and many Epeans on board. Their captains were Amphimachus and Thalpius—one the son of Cteatus, the other of Eurytus—both of the race of Actor. The other two were Diores, son of Amarynceus, and Polyxenus, son of King Agasthenes, son of Augeas.

And those of Dulichium and the sacred Echinean islands, who lived across the sea from Elis. Meges, peer of Ares, led them. He was the son of valiant Phyleus, who was dear to Zeus. Phyleus had quarreled with his father and gone to settle in Dulichium. Forty ships came with Meges.

Odysseus led the brave Cephallenians, who held Ithaca, Neritum with its forests, Crocylea, rugged Aegilips, Samos and Zacynthus, and the mainland across from the islands. Odysseus, peer of Zeus in counsel, led them, and twelve ships came with him.

Thoas, son of Andraemon, commanded the Aetolians, who lived in Pleuron, Olenus, Pylene, Chalcis by the sea, and rocky Calydon. The great king Oeneus now had no sons living, and he was dead himself, as was golden-haired Meleager, who had been set over the Aetolians as their king. Forty ships came with Thoas.

The famous spearsman Idomeneus led the Cretans, who held Cnossus and the well-walled city of Gortys; also Lyctus, Miletus and Lycastus on the chalk; the populous towns of Phaestus and Rhytium, with the other peoples who lived in the hundred cities of Crete. Idomeneus led them all, together with Meriones, peer of murderous Ares. Eighty ships came with these.

Tlepolemus, son of Heracles, a brave man and tall, brought nine ships of lordly warriors from Rhodes. His people lived in Rhodes, which is divided among the three cities of Lindus, Ielysus and Cameirus, which lies on the chalk. Tlepolemus, son of Heracles by Astyochea, commanded them. Heracles had carried her off from Ephyra, on the river Selleis, after sacking many cities of valiant warriors. When Tlepolemus grew up, he killed his father’s uncle Licymnius, who had been a famous warrior in his day but was now old. After this he built himself a fleet, gathered a great following and fled across the sea, because the other sons and grandsons of Heracles threatened him. After a voyage in which he suffered great hardship, he came to Rhodes. There the people divided into three communities, according to their tribes, and Zeus, the lord of gods and men, loved them dearly. So the son of Cronus showered great riches on them.
And Nireus brought three ships from Syme—Nireus, the handsomest man of all the Danaans who came to Ilium, after the son of Peleus. But he was a man of no substance and had only a small following.

Those who held Nisyrus, Crapathus and Casus, with Cos, the city of Eurypylus, and the Calydnian islands, were commanded by Pheidippus and Antiphus, two sons of King Thessalus the son of Heracles. Thirty ships came with them.

Then those who held Pelasgic Argos, Alos, Alope and Trachis, and those of Phthia and Hellas, the land of fair women, who were called Myrmidons, Hellenes and Achaeans: they had fifty ships, and Achilles was in command of them. But they now took no part in the war, because there was no one to marshal them. Achilles stayed by his ships, furious about the loss of the girl Briseis. He had taken her from Lyrnessus at great peril to himself, when he sacked Lyrnessus and Thebe and overthrew Mynes and Epistrophus, sons of king Evenor, son of Selepus. Achilles was still grieving for her sake, but before long he was to join them again.

And those who held Phylace and the flowery meadows of Pyrasus, sanctuary of Demeter; Iton, the mother of sheep; Antrum on the sea, and Pteleum, which lies on the grass lands. Brave Protesilaus had been their captain while he was alive, but now he lay under the earth. He had left a wife behind him in Phylace to tear her cheeks in sorrow, and his house was only half finished. A Dardanian warrior had slain him as he leaped foremost of the Achaeans onto the soil of Troy. Still, though his people mourned their chieftain, they were not without a leader. Podarces, of the race of Ares, marshalled them. He was the son of Iphiclus, rich in sheep, who was the son of Phylacus, and he was own brother to Protesilaus, only younger; Protesilaus was both the elder and the more valiant. So the people were not without a leader, though they mourned the man they had lost. Forty ships came with Podarces.

And those who held Pherae by the Boebean lake, with Boebe, Glaphyrae and the populous city of Iolcus, with their eleven ships, were led by Eumelus, son of Admetus. Alcestis bore him to Admetus; she was the loveliest of the daughters of Pelias.

And those who held Methone and Thaumacia, with Meliboea and rugged Olizon, were led by the skilled archer Philoctetes. They had seven ships, each with fifty oarsmen, all of them good archers. But Philoctetes was lying in great pain on the island of Lemnos, where the sons of the Achaeans had left him, because a poisonous water snake had bitten him. There he lay sick and sorry, and before long the Argives would come to miss him. But his people, though they felt his loss, were not leaderless. Medon, the bastard son of Oileus by Rhene, set them in array.

Then the men of Tricca and the stony region of Ithome, and those who held Oechalia, the city of Oechalian Eurytus, were commanded by the two sons of Asclepius, Podalirius and Machaon, who were skilled in the art of healing. Thirty ships came with them.
Also the men of Ormenius, and by the fountain of Hypereia, with those who held Asterius and the white crests of Titanus, were led by Eurypylus, the son of Euaemon. Forty ships came with them.

Those who held Argissa and Gyrtone, Orthe, Elone and the white city of Oloosson had brave Polypoetes as their leader. He was the son of Pirithous, who was himself a son of Zeus. Hippodameia bore Polypoetes to Pirithous on the day when Pirithous took his revenge on the shaggy mountain savages and drove them from Mount Pelion to the Aithices. But Polypoetes was not the sole commander. With him was Leonteus, of the race of Ares, son of Coronus, the son of Caeneus. Forty ships came with these.

Guneus brought twenty-two ships from Cyphus. The Enienes and the valiant Peraebi followed him, who lived around wintry Dodona and held the lands around the lovely river Titaresius, which sends its waters into the Peneus. The Titaresius does not mingle with the silver eddies of the Peneus but flows on top of them like oil, because it is a branch of dread Orcus and of the river Styx.
Prothous son of Tenthredon commanded the Magnetes. They lived around the river Peneus and Mount Pelion. Swift-footed Prothous was their leader, and forty ships came with him.
That was the list of the chiefs and princes of the Danaans. Now tell me, O Muse: among the men who followed the sons of Atreus, who was the best, and which was the best horse?

Of the horses, those of the son of Pheres were by far the finest. Eumelus drove them, and they were as swift as birds. They were the same age and color, and perfectly matched in height. Apollo, god of the silver bow, had bred them in Perea. Both were mares, and terrible as Ares in battle. Of the men, Ajax son of Telamon was much the foremost as long as Achilles’s anger lasted, for Achilles excelled him greatly and also had better horses. But Achilles was now holding aloof at his ships because of his quarrel with Agamemnon. His people passed their time on the seashore, throwing discs, aiming spears at a mark, and shooting with the bow. Their horses stood each by his own chariot, champing lotus and wild celery. The chariots were housed under cover, but their owners, for lack of a leader, wandered here and there about the host and did not go out to fight.

So the host marched like a consuming fire, and the earth groaned beneath them, as it does when the lord of thunder is angry and lashes the land around Typhoeus among the Arimi, where they say Typhoeus lies. In the same way the earth groaned beneath them as they sped over the plain.

Meanwhile Zeus sent Iris, swift as the wind, to carry the bad news to the Trojans. Old and young, they were holding an assembly at Priam’s gates. Iris went right up to Priam and spoke in the voice of his son Polites. Polites was swift-footed, and the Trojans had posted him as their watchman on the tomb of old Aesyetes, to look out for any sally by the Achaeans. In his likeness Iris said: “Old man, you talk on and on as if it were peacetime, but war is upon us. I have fought in many battles, yet I have never seen an army like the one now advancing. They are crossing the plain to attack the city, as thick as leaves or as the sands of the sea. Hector, I charge you above all others to do what I say. Allies are scattered all through the city of Priam, men from distant places who speak different tongues. Each chief must give orders to his own people, set them in array separately, and lead them out to battle.”

The goddess had spoken, and Hector knew it. He broke up the assembly at once. The men ran for their arms, every gate was thrown open, and the people poured out, horse and foot, with the tramp of a great multitude.

Before the city, apart from everything else, a high mound rises on the plain. Men call it Batieia, but the gods know it as the tomb of lithe Myrine. The Trojans and their allies divided their forces here.
Great Hector of the gleaming helmet, Priam’s son, commanded the Trojans. By far the greater number, and the most valiant of those who longed for the fray, were drawn up with him.

Brave Aeneas led the Dardanians. Aphrodite bore him to Anchises, when she, goddess though she was, lay with him on the mountain slopes of Ida. He was not alone: with him were the two sons of Antenor, Archelochus and Acamas, both skilled in all the arts of war.

Those who lived in Telea under the lowest spurs of Mount Ida, men of substance who drink the limpid waters of the Aesepus and are of Trojan blood—Pandarus son of Lycaon led them, and Apollo had taught him to use the bow.

Adrestus and Amphius led the men who held Adresteia and the land of Apaesus, with Pityeia and the high mountain of Tereia. Amphius wore a breastplate of linen. The two were sons of Merops of Percote, who excelled in every kind of divination. He told them not to join the war, but they ignored him, because fate was luring them to destruction.

Those who lived around Percote and Practius, with Sestos, Abydos and Arisbe—Asius, son of Hyrtacus, a brave commander, led them. Asius, the son of Hyrtacus, had come from Arisbe, brought by his powerful dark bay horses of the breed from the river Selleis.
The Pelasgian spearsmen of fertile Larissa had two leaders, Hippothous and Pylaeus of the race of Ares. They were the two sons of the Pelasgian Lethus, son of Teutamus.
Acamas and the warrior Peirous commanded the Thracians and those who came from beyond the mighty stream of the Hellespont.
Euphemus, son of Troezenus, the son of Ceos, was captain of the Ciconian spearsmen.
Pyraechmes led the Paeonian archers from distant Amydon, by the broad waters of the river Axius, the fairest that flow on the earth.

Stout-hearted Pylaemanes commanded the Paphlagonians, from Enetae, where the mules run wild in herds. They held Cytorus and the country around Sesamus, with the cities by the river Parthenius, Cromna, Aegialus and lofty Erithini.
Odius and Epistrophus were captains over the Halizoni from distant Alybe, where there are mines of silver.

Chromis and Ennomus the augur led the Mysians. But his skill in augury did not save Ennomus from destruction. He fell by the hand of the swift descendant of Aeacus in the river, who killed other Trojans there as well.
Phorcys and noble Ascanius led the Phrygians from the far country of Ascania, and both were eager for the fray.
Mesthles and Antiphus commanded the Meonians. They were sons of Talaemenes, born to him of the Gygaean lake. They led the Meonians, who lived under Mount Tmolus.

Nastes led the Carians, men of a strange speech. They held Miletus and the wooded mountain of Phthires, the water of the river Maeander and the lofty crests of Mount Mycale. Their commanders were Nastes and Amphimachus, the brave sons of Nomion. Nastes went into the fight wearing gold, like a girl. The fool gained nothing from it. He fell in the river to the swift descendant of Aeacus, and Achilles carried his gold away.
Sarpedon and Glaucus led the Lycians from their distant land, by the eddying waters of the Xanthus.
